abstract: One of the mechanisms by which the circadian clock influences plant growth and development is through modulating gene expression timing under light/dark cycles. While wild potato accessions display significant variation in their circadian period, cultivated accessions possess fast clocks independent of their geographic origin. Here, we explore the implications of variation in circadian period on diel gene expression by comparing a short-period cultivar of Solanum tuberosum with two wild potato species, the short-period S. candolleanum and the long-period S. chacoense, through transcriptomics. In all three species, the diel phase of clock-associated genes is well-correlated to the pace of the clock. However, S. tuberosum displays a significant genome-wide delay in gene expression phase despite its short circadian period. This delayed phase was also observed in both diel leaf movements and sucrose content. Reconstruction of the transcriptional network indicates that DOF and REVEILLE transcription factors play a major role in diel expression patterns in these species. In modern cultivated potatoes, truncated alleles of the DOF transcription factor CYCLING DOF FACTOR 1 enable early tuberization. We find that CDF1 is able to repress RVE1a expression in vivo. We propose that truncated CDF1, in combination with its downstream targets, leads to delays in gene expression that are decoupled of circadian control.
